newsitem.title: USA: Gold lowest in more than three years, seen even lower.
newsitem.headline: Gold lowest in more than three years, seen even lower.

text.p: The price of gold fell to its lowest level in more than three years Monday as investors cold-shouldered the metal in favour of booming stock markets, and some analysts said gold may be teetering on the brink of an even bigger slide.

On New York's Commodity Exchange, the active February gold contract closed down $3.30 to $358.70 an ounce after tumbling $4.60 on Friday. The last time gold traded at current levels was in early October 1993, when it hovered at $350.00.

"This is the first week of the new year and we're at three-year lows," said Ted Arnold, an analyst at Merrill Lynch in London. "Increasingly it looks like the downside is wide open. In 1997, I think $330 looks possible."

Investors have seen little reason to put money in gold, a traditional "safe haven," as inflation in the United States -- the world's biggest economy -- remains in check and stock prices are near record highs.

"There was a good deal of call option activity pre-Christmas but the year-end bounce failed to occur, forcing a lot of people to cover positions and go short again," said Andre DiMino, an analyst at Apostle Capital Management in New Jersey.
The precious metal is also being dogged by commodity fund traders who have sold gold "short" in anticipation of still-lower prices.
In London bullion was fixed at $359.25 an ounce, the lowest since Oct. 7, 1993 and down sharply from Friday afternoon's fixing of $364.00.
Heavy selling Friday by speculative investment funds sent prices reeling as a strong dollar and buoyant stock and bond markets pulled money out of gold.
Gold continued losing ground in European trading Monday. It has been sinking since coming off a rally last February when it hit a high of $416.00.

Physical demand remains soft, while uncertainty continues about the role of gold in the new single European currency system due in 1999, and the potential for further European central bank gold sales in 1997, analysts said.

European central banks hold 460 million ounces of gold -- 40 percent of all official holdings worldwide -- but have not decided what to do with their reserves when they surrender their monetary policy powers to the planned European central bank.
Technical analysts said that price charts pointed to more erosion in the price of gold.
"Selling pressure has increased across this complex, forcing new lows," said Elli Gifford, technical analyst at Investment Research. "Despite oversold considerations, further falls are likely."
Some dealers put initial support for gold at around $358.00, while the brokerage house Rudolf Wolff said there was little propping up values above $350.
